lead: Three unit processes put material and dopant where a transistor needs them. Oxidation grows silicon dioxide that insulates, masks and protects. Diffusion moves dopant atoms into the crystal with heat. Ion implantation fires dopants in at a set energy and dose, so the depth is chosen in keV. The gate oxide, the wells and the source-drain junctions of every CMOS flow come from these steps.
prereq: You need: donors, acceptors and the MOS structure. The mask window is opened in the chapter on lithography, etching and deposition.

blocks.text: Silicon oxidises into a dense, stable insulator that sticks to the silicon beneath it, so one material gives both the semiconductor and its insulator. SiO<sub>2</sub> serves as the gate insulator, as field insulator between devices, and as a mask that dopants cannot pass.

Thermal oxidation runs in a furnace at 900–1100 °C. Dry oxidation uses oxygen: Si + O<sub>2</sub> → SiO<sub>2</sub>. Wet oxidation uses steam: Si + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → SiO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>. Wet growth is many times faster and makes the thick field oxide. Dry growth is slow and dense and makes the thin gate oxide, where a few nanometres set the threshold voltage (see Threshold voltage and body effect).

blocks.where: x<sub>ox</sub> is the oxide thickness in μm; t is the time in hours; A (μm) and B (μm²/h) depend on temperature and on the gas; τ allows for oxide already present. This is the Deal-Grove model.

items: Thin oxide: x<sub>ox</sub> ≈ (B/A)(t + τ). The surface reaction limits growth, so it is linear in time.
Thick oxide: x<sub>ox</sub> ≈ √(B·t). The oxidant must diffuse through the oxide already grown, so growth slows to a square root.
Growing 1 μm of oxide uses about 0.44 μm of silicon; the rest of the film rises above the old surface.
Gate oxide is dry, often 2–10 nm; field oxide is wet, 0.2–1 μm.

blocks.text: A dopant atom hops at random between lattice sites, but a concentration gradient makes more hops go downhill. Fick's first law gives the flux: J = −D(∂C/∂x), with J in atoms cm⁻² s⁻¹, D the diffusion coefficient in cm²/s, C the concentration in cm⁻³ and x the depth. Conservation of atoms gives Fick's second law, ∂C/∂t = D(∂²C/∂x²).

blocks.where: D<sub>0</sub> is the pre-exponential factor, in cm²/s like D; E<sub>a</sub> is the activation energy, about 3–4 eV for common dopants; k = 8.62×10⁻⁵ eV/K; T is in kelvin. Near 1000 °C, D roughly doubles for every 30 °C, so furnace temperature sets junction depth.

blocks.text: A doping step has two parts. Predeposition holds the wafer in a dopant gas: the surface sits at the solid solubility and a complementary error function (erfc) profile with a fixed dose Q forms. Drive-in removes the source and heats the wafer further: the dose spreads deeper as a Gaussian and the surface concentration falls.

blocks.where: C is the concentration in cm⁻³ at depth x; Q is the dose in cm⁻². The surface value is C<sub>s</sub> = Q/√(πDt); at one diffusion length, x = L = 2√(Dt), the concentration has fallen to C<sub>s</sub>/e.

blocks.text: x<sub>j</sub> is the junction depth, where the dopant equals the wafer's background doping N<sub>B</sub>. It is usually two to three diffusion lengths, so L and x<sub>j</sub> are different numbers.
Diffusion is isotropic: dopant spreads sideways under a mask edge nearly as far as it goes down, about 0.8 xj. Layout must leave room for this, and the layout design rules encode it.

sections.h3: Ion implantation: placing dopants by energy

blocks.text: Diffusion cannot make a doping that is shallow, heavy and precisely placed; implantation can. Dopant ions are accelerated through tens to hundreds of keV and fired at the wafer, where nuclear collisions and electronic drag stop them at a depth set by the energy.

The dose φ is the number of ions per area, typically 10¹¹ to 10¹⁶ cm⁻², counted from the beam current. The average stopping depth is the projected range R<sub>p</sub>, and the spread around it is the straggle ΔR<sub>p</sub>.
C(x) is in cm⁻³ at depth x; φ is in cm⁻²; R<sub>p</sub> and ΔR<sub>p</sub> are in cm. The peak, at x = R<sub>p</sub>, is about 0.4φ/ΔR<sub>p</sub>.

If the beam lines up with a crystal channel, ions travel far deeper and leave a tail, so the wafer is tilted about 7° and rotated. A mask must be about R<sub>p</sub> + 4ΔR<sub>p</sub> thick to block the implant; one just thicker than R<sub>p</sub> lets almost half the dose through. When the poly gate is the mask, source and drain line up with its edge without a separate alignment: a self-aligned implant.

The collisions leave a damaged, partly amorphous layer. A short anneal near 900–1000 °C repairs the lattice and moves dopants onto lattice sites, which activates them; too long or too hot an anneal diffuses the profile away.

examples.question: A predeposition puts a phosphorus dose Q = 1×10¹⁴ cm⁻² into a p-type wafer doped N<sub>B</sub> = 1×10¹⁶ cm⁻³. It is then driven in at 1000 °C, where D = 3×10⁻¹⁴ cm²/s, for t = 1 hour. (a) Find the diffusion length L = 2√(Dt). (b) Find the surface concentration after the drive-in. (c) Find the junction depth x<sub>j</sub>. (d) Is the junction deeper or shallower than 0.5 μm, and why is x<sub>j</sub> not equal to L?
steps: Time in seconds: t = 1 h = 3600 s. Then D·t = 3×10⁻¹⁴ cm²/s × 3600 s = 1.08×10⁻¹⁰ cm².
(c) The junction is where C(x<sub>j</sub>) = N<sub>B</sub>. C<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>B</sub> = 5.43×10¹⁸ / 1×10¹⁶ = 543; ln 543 = 6.30; √6.30 = 2.51.
(d) 0.522 μm is just deeper than 0.5 μm. At x = L the dopant is still C<sub>s</sub>/e = 2.0×10¹⁸ cm⁻³, 200 times the background; the type changes only at 2.51 L.
Check: (x<sub>j</sub>/L)² = (0.522/0.208)² = 6.30 = ln 543, so C(x<sub>j</sub>) = C<sub>s</sub>/543 = 1.0×10¹⁶ cm⁻³.
examples.answer: L = 0.21 μm, C<sub>s</sub> = 5.4×10¹⁸ cm⁻³ and x<sub>j</sub> = 0.52 μm, just deeper than 0.5 μm. The junction lies 2.5 diffusion lengths down because the dopant must fall all the way to the background doping, not just to 1/e of its surface value.

examples.question: Boron is implanted into an n-well doped N<sub>D</sub> = 1×10¹⁷ cm⁻³ with dose φ = 1×10¹⁵ cm⁻², R<sub>p</sub> = 0.10 μm and ΔR<sub>p</sub> = 0.03 μm. (a) Find the peak concentration. (b) Find the depth of the p-n junction under the implant. (c) Taking the range in oxide as close to the range in silicon, how thick must an oxide mask be to block the implant elsewhere?
steps: (b) Below the peak the boron falls to the well doping where C<sub>p</sub>·exp(−(x − R<sub>p</sub>)²/2ΔR<sub>p</sub>²) = N<sub>D</sub>.
x<sub>j</sub> = 0.10 + 0.114 = 0.214 μm. The surface value, 5.1×10¹⁷ cm⁻³, is also above N<sub>D</sub>, so the layer is p-type from the surface down.
(c) Mask thickness ≥ R<sub>p</sub> + 4ΔR<sub>p</sub> = 0.10 + 4 × 0.03 = 0.22 μm of oxide.
examples.answer: Peak 1.33×10²⁰ cm⁻³ at 0.10 μm; junction at 0.214 μm; an oxide mask about 0.22 μm thick blocks the implant.

traps: Dose is per area (cm⁻²); concentration is per volume (cm⁻³). A 10¹⁵ cm⁻² implant spread over 0.1 μm gives about 10²⁰ cm⁻³, not 10¹⁵ cm⁻³.
L = 2√(Dt) is not the junction depth. The junction is where the dopant falls to the background doping, x<sub>j</sub> = L·√ln(C<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>B</sub>), usually two to three times L.
Wet oxide is fast and thick, dry oxide is slow and dense. Gate oxide is dry, field oxide is wet — not the other way round.
Deal-Grove: linear for thin oxide (reaction-limited), parabolic for thick (diffusion-limited). Examiners deliberately swap the two labels.

quiz.q: Why does oxide growth slow down as the film gets thicker?
quiz.a: The oxidant must reach the silicon by diffusing through the oxide already grown. In the thick-film limit that diffusion, not the surface reaction, limits the rate, so x<sub>ox</sub> grows as √(B·t) instead of linearly.

quiz.q: Dry oxidation at 1000 °C has A = 0.165 μm and B = 0.0117 μm²/h. Ignoring τ, how long does a 10 nm gate oxide take, and how far off is the linear limit?
quiz.a: Exact: t = (0.0001 + 0.00165)/0.0117 = 0.150 h ≈ 9.0 min. Linear: B/A = 0.0709 μm/h, t = 0.01/0.0709 = 0.141 h ≈ 8.5 min, 6 % short, so the linear limit is close enough.

quiz.q: A wet field oxidation gives 0.2 μm; 0.5 μm is wanted. In the parabolic regime (x² = B·t), by what factor must the total time grow, and how much extra time is that?
quiz.a: t grows as x², so the total time must be (0.5/0.2)² = 6.25 times the first run. The extra time is 5.25 times the first run.

quiz.q: Why is the wafer tilted about 7° during implantation?
quiz.a: To prevent channeling. If the beam is parallel to a major crystal direction, ions travel between atom rows and stop far deeper than R<sub>p</sub>, leaving an unwanted tail; the tilt plus a rotation closes every channel.

quiz.q: What is the difference between predeposition and drive-in?
quiz.a: Predeposition keeps a dopant source on the surface at a lower temperature, so a fixed dose enters at the solubility limit. Drive-in removes the source and raises the temperature, so the existing dopants spread deeper and the surface concentration drops.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern fabs run these steps for seconds: rapid thermal oxidation, spike anneals and millisecond laser anneals keep a 20 nm junction where it was put. A 1 nm oxide leaks by tunnelling, so the gate insulator is now nitrided oxide or high-k HfO<sub>2</sub>. Search for rapid thermal processing, high-k metal gate and plasma doping.
